oewn-05167108-n.learner: It is the help or advantage that something brings.
examples: She only said it for your own good.
I gave up sweets for the good of my health.

oewn-04856472-n.learner: It is the quality of being morally right and worth admiring.
examples: She believed there was still good in him.

oewn-05149427-n.learner: It is whatever is pleasing, or valuable, or useful.
examples: You must weigh the good against the bad before you decide.

oewn-00429255-n.learner: It is taking a series of steps and movements in time with music.
examples: Such very superior dancing is not often seen.
Indeed, sir, I have not the least intention of dancing.

oewn-13758939-n.learner: It is one of the two equal parts that something can be divided into.
examples: The two elder Miss Bennets were able to be for half an hour by themselves.
She cut the cake and gave him half.

oewn-15282640-n.learner: It is one of the two parts that a game or a performance is split into, with a break between them.
examples: The scores were level at the end of the first half.

oewn-00011555-r.learner: It means in a good, proper, or satisfactory way, or up to a high standard.
examples: The baby can walk pretty good now.
He speaks English good enough to get by.
We beat them good.
The rain soaked us good.

oewn-05165478-n.learner: It is the giving of a favour or an advantage to one person or country over another.
examples: But you are always giving her the preference.
I cannot help giving him the preference even over Wickham.

oewn-07513449-n.learner: It is a strong liking for something.
examples: He had been gratifying his vanity by encouraging the preference which she believed she had most incautiously shown.

oewn-06210079-n.learner: It is a leaning inside you that makes you favour one thing.
examples: Most readers come to a story with a preference for happy endings.

oewn-01791774-v.learner: To make someone annoyed, or to bother them with small irritations.
examples: You take delight in vexing me.
It vexed her to see him expose himself to such a man.

oewn-01769760-v.learner: To take away someone's peace of mind, and fill them with worry or distress.
examples: It would vex me, indeed, to see you again the dupe of Miss Bingley's pretended regard.

oewn-00624056-v.learner: To be a mystery to someone, so that they cannot understand.
examples: The riddle vexed him for hours; he could not see the answer.

oewn-02344427-a.learner: Small in amount, so that it cannot meet a need or a requirement.
examples: The interest of one thousand pounds would be a very insufficient support.
Four sides of paper were insufficient to contain all her delight.

oewn-01471597-a.learner: Having bad luck, or bringing bad luck.
examples: He has been so unlucky as to lose your friendship.
I am particularly unlucky in meeting with a person so well able to expose my real character.

oewn-01055109-s.learner: Showing bad fortune, or promising bad fortune to come.
examples: The unlucky ship sailed out that morning and was never seen again.

oewn-00295773-r.learner: As a result of what came before.
examples: Mr. Bingley was obliged to be in town the following day, and consequently unable to accept the honour of their invitation.
She was, consequently, resolved not to be out of sight of the inn.

oewn-00063395-r.learner: It joins one sentence to another, and means: because of the reason just given.
examples: Consequently, he did not do it.
Consequently, the meeting was put off until Monday.

oewn-00047930-r.learner: To a degree that goes past normal or proper limits.
examples: He talks excessively, long after everyone else wants to leave.
She worries excessively about things that will never happen.
